issues.legal_issue: A subordinate court does not commit contempt by acting contrary to a superior court order unless it had knowledge of the order from an authorised or otherwise authentic source and intentionally disobeyed it.
material_facts: A superior court stayed proceedings before a subordinate court, but did not direct that the stay order be communicated to that court by telegram.

Before the subordinate court acted, it received an application with an illegible signature and no supporting affidavit, together with a telegram whose sender and authority to communicate the stay were not established.
The subordinate court allowed an application for restitution before receiving an official copy of the stay order.
After an official copy of the stay order arrived, the subordinate court stayed further proceedings and did not permit a writ for redelivery of possession to issue.
The superior court convicted the subordinate court's magistrate of contempt and imposed a fine.
issues.conclusion: The magistrate was not guilty of contempt because he had no sufficiently authoritative or authentic knowledge of the stay order when he acted. The conviction and fine were set aside.
issues.legal_principle: Disobedience of a superior court order by a subordinate court is contempt only when the subordinate court knew of the order and intentionally disobeyed it. Knowledge must come from an authorised or otherwise authentic source; action in ignorance of the order, or accidental disobedience, is not contempt. The judgment identifies no statutory provision or earlier case as the basis for this principle.

predicates.subordinate_court_contempt_proceeding: A contempt proceeding alleges that a subordinate court disobeyed an order of a superior court.
predicates.no_authoritative_knowledge_when_act_occu: The subordinate court had not learned of the order, before acting, from a source that was authorised or otherwise authentic.
predicates.no_contempt_for_order_disobedience: The subordinate court's act does not constitute contempt for disobeying the order.

issues.definition: When a contempt proceeding concerns a subordinate court's alleged disobedience and that court lacked authoritative knowledge of the order when it acted, the rule treats the disobedience as no contempt.

issues.legal_issue: Judges who decide a contempt matter should not be made parties to a proceeding challenging that decision when no relief is claimed against them.
material_facts: The magistrate appealed his contempt conviction and named the Chief Justice and judges of the court that convicted him as respondents.
No relief was claimed against those judges; they had decided the contempt matter in their judicial capacity.
The court noted the English practice of styling such proceedings as being in re the alleged contemnor and referred to the differing party practice in Ambard v. Attorney-General for Trinidad & Tobago.
issues.conclusion: The Chief Justice and judges should not be made parties to a contempt proceeding or an appeal from it when no relief is claimed against them; the proceeding should be titled in re the alleged contemnor. The existing practice of joining the judges should be discontinued.
issues.legal_principle: Parties to a suit or appeal are those who claim relief, against whom relief is given or sought, or who have a right to be heard because of an interest in the result. Judges who decide a contempt matter have no such litigant's interest merely by virtue of their decision. The court endorsed the English practice of using an in re title and referred to Ambard v. Attorney-General for Trinidad & Tobago as an example of a different party practice in an appeal.

predicates.contempt_proceeding: The proceeding concerns an alleged contempt of court or a challenge to a contempt decision.
predicates.no_relief_claimed_against_judges: No party seeks relief against the judges who decided the contempt matter.
predicates.judges_not_parties_and_title_identifies_: The deciding judges are not joined as parties, and the proceeding is titled to identify the alleged contemnor.

issues.definition: When a contempt proceeding involves judges against whom no relief is sought, the rule excludes them as parties and identifies the alleged contemnor in the title.
